A51.description:
Determinative for revered persons, and ideogram for +tSpsi "be noble".
According to Fischer, o.c., the normal ideogram for +tSpsi is A50-,
and A51- was originaly a name determinative for kings (beginning of dyn. XII),
then individuals. It then could be used for +tSpsi as well (early example under Sesostris III).
!
The description given by Gardiner o.c. gives +tSpsi as primary value, and the determinative as
a secondary development, which doesn't fit the available data.
!
A line example with value +tSpsi- (probably FIP) can be found in  Callender, o.c. p. 25 (§ 38).
Note that the example in Callender is quite peculiar, and is in fact closer to A51C-, and comes in a specific setting.
!
Bibliography
V. G. Callender, El-hawawish, Tombs, Sarcophagi, Stelae Palaeography PalHier 8, p. 25
H. G. Fischer, Ancient Egyptian Calligraphy, p. 17
A. H.Gardiner Egyptian Grammar, p. 447

A63.description:
NOTE: we have two different signs here. This notice should be cut in two, and another sign 
should be created.
!
King seated on a throne and holding the +tmdw stick.
The Gardiner shape has a little guard in the middle of the stick.
Attested already in the Old Kingdom, but known afterwards. The sign came in the Gardiner fonts because 
of the edition of the Abydos Temple.
!
Seems to be the sign discussed in Farout, o.c., but with a different scepter (a +tHD mace instead of a
+tHkA sign) and no triangular apron. 
The apron does not appear in Gardiner's version of the sign,
but was in the Hieroglyphica.
!
Further inquiry is needed to see if we have more than one sign here (maybe diachronic evolution).
For Farout, the sign, (which holds  S43- and HD- in the O.K. versions he discusses), is often found after the king's name
in the particular context of royal decrees.
Det. +tHms, to sit, for a king. (or +tsnDm)
Abydos, Sethos Temple, stairway passage, dyn. XIX.
!
Gardiner notes that the insignia may vary.
!
Bibliography

Farout, D. "les déclarations du roi Ounas", in RdE 65, p. 54.+s

A342.description:
If I don't mix signs, this one should display an hippopotamus and not a pig (according to Y. Guermeur, op.cit.)
Value +txsdb, lapis-lazuli, from an hypothetic word play : +txwsi-sd-db ^"shake the tail of the hippopotamus".
From a look in the original Manuel de Codage
Two examples are given.
One with filled (black) signs. The animal is a bit difficult to recognize,
but is maybe more an hippopotamus than a pig.
The other one is in light font (XIXth century font?), and definitly shows a pig. (A257- A257)
Now, in Guermeur's article, it's definitly an hippopotamus.
Three possibilities:
a) those are two different signs
b) there was an error at some point in font making.
c) there are variants of the sign. Leitz, Quellentexte, lists them both. 
Bibliography
Y. Guermeur, "à propos de l'épigraphie Ptolémaïque", Égypte, Afrique et Orient 46 (2007), p. 32.+s

I96.description:
(from JSesh web site, in answer to a question about this sign)
Probably a bug in hieroglyphica for I96VARA-!
The Hieroglyphica contains exactly this shape you found for I96 and I136.
I searched in the "Valeurs phonetiques", and found only two very similar signs (Volume I, p. 201, signs 1051 and 1053),
with refs. Junker, Abaton p. 84, Bénédite, Philae, p. 63, 7; 119 5 and 7.
The equivalent of I136 I136- is documented in Sauneron, BIFAO 62, 1964, p. 17
(which is available on the web on the IFAO site). Those signs have value "jnḏ", but the snake looks like a I9 without horns.
In fact, it's probably to be understood more as a I10. A look at the original "Manuel de Codage" book
(which shows glyphs from various sources, mainly lead fonts from the XIXth and XXth century printer shop
before computerized hieroglyphs, plus handwritten hieroglyphs from the WB archives),
seems to indicate that indeed the I96 and I136 signs should not have horns.
When going from the original MdC description to the hieroglyphica computer font,
the sign was probably thought to be an "I9 on legs", as it looks like one.
 The JSesh glyph form was, as usually for most composed signs, created on the basis of the Hieroglyphica,
which only gives a picture of the sign.
It definitely shows that computer hieroglyphic fonts should be documented, and the sign described, to avoid such problems.
Anyway, thanks for pointing out this sign...

scribe expose les misères du laboureur et lui dit de son blé que t:A-k:A-kA:1-t:I14-

drawn horizontally as O31-. One would expect O31\R270-orO31\R90-. The fine remark made by Lacau

déterminatif de sa propre lecture") when used in wn:n-O31-+twn, to open.

geometry, has different meanings (the most obvious case is D54-and D55-, but 
the MdC gives them different codes).
